beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City family talks; Isaias at Panhandle landfall.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Day three of the Amoris Laetitia anniversary meeting focused on young people and the vocation to marriage. Cardinal Kevin Farrell opened with falling marriage rates worldwide; bishops discussed accompanying cohabiting couples without indifference or condemnation, and married couples from Couples for Christ shared witness. A Holy See Press Office briefing also named the commission that will draft the Oct. 14 summary report.

Africa. Ethiopia and Eritrea traded Friday accusations of launching a war of aggression. Addis Ababa’s UN letter called Eritrea’s advance into Tigray an “all-out invasion”; Asmara’s information minister said Ethiopia has been pursuing war for Red Sea access and denied backing the TPLF. Ethiopian forces hold Mekelle; Ethiopian Airlines plans flights there Oct. 11. Security sources told AFP roughly 5,000–8,000 Eritrean soldiers may be in Tigray.

Asia. Saudi civil aviation said Riyadh’s King Khalid airport is back to normal after Thursday’s Houthi strikes that killed three Saudis, including a Saudia captain. The Saudi-led coalition vowed a “firm response” and said it destroyed Houthi missile launch platforms. The Houthis again warned airlines about Saudi airspace; oil and Hormuz diplomacy remain tense with no new U.S. strike before the midterms.

Europe. In Miami, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner opened two-day talks with Ukrainian negotiators (including Kyrylo Budanov and Rustem Umerov) and European, NATO, and EU officials—Russia is not at the table. Washington is pitching “new ideas,” including a possible limited pause on energy and grain attacks, toward a unified proposal that could go to Moscow later this month.

North America. Hurricane Isaias is making landfall this evening near Destin on the western Florida Panhandle as a Category 2, with hurricane-force winds already ashore (gusts near 97 mph at Gulf Breeze) and an extreme wind warning for Pensacola–Destin. Life-threatening surge and inland flooding remain the main threats; South Florida is not in the hurricane warning. Operators have shut in about 71.5% of U.S. Gulf oil production (~1.46 million bpd) and nearly 59% of Gulf gas. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast, Hurricane Simon strengthened to 110 mph about 190 miles south of Manzanillo and is forecast to become a major hurricane before nearing west-central Mexico late Saturday or Sunday.

South America. Authorities overflew Santiago’s Las Condes on Friday after Thursday’s flash mudflow in San Carlos de Apoquindo left six injured, more than a thousand assisted, and thousands of homes with mud or water damage; officials are probing a blocked drainage channel and saturated slopes. Brazil’s runoff and the Eduardo Bolsonaro arrest order stand as this morning noted.

Oceania. Quiet since this morning on the New Zealand campaign and Australia–NZ Lone Wolf raids.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: RFK Jr. vaccine-injury clinic; HHS kratom thresholds.
beats.body:
“Make America Healthy Again” — vaccine injury transparency. What was done: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a new NIH clinic focused on identifying and treating reported vaccine complications, plus steps to modernize adverse-event reporting and possibly compensate doctors for filing reports. An internal memo obtained by NPR says the clinic will follow vaccinated people and may review federal schedules. Impact: vaccine-safety researchers welcome more rigorous science but warn fishing expeditions or incentivized reporting could inflate spurious findings just as measles and other preventable diseases are resurging and top officials stay largely silent on vaccine benefits.

Target enhanced kratom opioids, spare botanical leaf. What was done: HHS today recommended DEA concentration and ratio thresholds so temporary Schedule I control of 7-OH and MGPI hits concentrated or chemically altered “enhanced” products while leaving natural botanical kratom with only trace alkaloids outside that net; DOJ said DEA issued matching Notices of Intent. Impact: this is a concrete MAHA-style line between addiction-risk synthetics and a popular herbal product—policy detail activists often say they want—while the morning’s broader food/pesticide scorecard fight continues unchanged.

Investors also weighed Musk’s clarification that Tesla and SpaceX will own and operate the planned Texas Terafab chip campus (initial phase roughly $10–20 billion) ahead of Oct. 21 earnings. Forbes put Musk’s net worth back above $1 trillion (~$1.012T) on the SpaceX–Tesla rally.

SpaceX / Starlink Mobile. Friday trading digested Thursday’s Grain Management 800 MHz spectrum deal: SpaceX shares were around $163 mid-day Friday; T-Mobile fell about 11% and AT&T about 7% as traders priced a future U.S. carrier rival. SpaceX says the low-band licenses (still needing FCC approval) are the “last critical piece” for Starlink Mobile’s in-building coverage with existing handsets.

beats.title: NASA
beats.headline: NASA opens private space-station RFP; CRS-35 still Oct. 13.
beats.body:
NASA on Friday released its long-awaited Commercial LEO Destinations request for proposals—about 360 pages—asking U.S. industry to build private space stations that could host NASA crews as early as 2030 after the ISS retires. Administrator Jared Isaacman said NASA will never give up low-Earth orbit; Phase 1 winners get at least $100 million, responses are due Dec. 8, and selections are targeted for April. Expected bidders include Axiom, Voyager/Starlab, and Vast; NASA is offering to help furnish early crew/cargo flights (pricing estimates around $325 million for a four-seat crew flight in 2030).

CRS-35 remains targeted for Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:33 a.m. ET from Cape Canaveral with more than 6,300 pounds of cargo and the final ISS roll-out solar arrays, docking about Oct. 15. Crew-12’s Thursday splashdown coverage stands; no new post-flight science dump since morning.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Tagle named Dean; Isaias nears Panhandle landfall.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, 69, the Filipino pro-prefect for first evangelization, was elected Dean of the College of Cardinals on Thursday by the cardinal-bishops and announced today, succeeding 92-year-old Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, who becomes Dean Emeritus after nearly seven years. Tagle keeps Albano and takes Ostia; the Dean’s main duty is to convene and, if under 80, preside at a conclave. Yesterday evening Pope Leo celebrated Mass in St. Peter’s to open the pontifical universities’ year, urging reason and critical thinking against “false teachers.” The Amoris Laetitia family meeting continues; today’s theme is young people and the vocation to marriage, with a 1:30 p.m. Rome briefing.

Africa. Ethiopia told the UN that Eritrean forces have advanced up to 60 km into northern Tigray in what it called an “all-out invasion,” after ACLED and local reports of Eritrean troops near Adigrat and drone strikes on them. The neighbors cut diplomatic ties last week. Kenya still reports one imported Bundibugyo Ebola death and about 57 contacts; Somalia formed a six-ministry committee to prepare. Congo’s outbreak remains the largest on record, with more than 8,000 cases and over 4,000 deaths. In Durban, clashes near a refugee reception centre scattered asylum seekers and prompted a U.S. consulate safety alert.

Asia. President Trump said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms and claimed “productive discussions” with Tehran; oil eased. Iran’s foreign minister says Tehran is reviewing Washington’s reply to its seven-day Hormuz reopening plan. Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport killed three Saudis, including Saudia captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami; the Saudi-led coalition vowed a “firm” response, and flights have largely resumed. CENTCOM says Hormuz traffic continues, including about 20 million barrels of crude. China nominated Song Li, its women-and-children’s health chief, to lead the WHO.

Europe. Russian strikes killed two and wounded five in Zaporizhzhia Friday, part of a three-day toll above 50 across Ukraine after the Kramatorsk bus strike. Ukrainian and European officials are flying to Miami for U.S.-led talks with envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on a possible energy and Black Sea pause; Russia is not at the table. In France, school blockades continue. In Britain, Able Seaman Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young appeared in court on National Security Act charges alleging he prepared to spy for Russia; the case goes to the Old Bailey on October 16.

North America. Hurricane Isaias is near 110 mph about 200 miles south of the Mississippi mouth and is expected to briefly become a major hurricane before landfall tonight or early Saturday as a high-end Category 2 between Mobile and Fort Walton Beach, with life-threatening surge from the Mississippi mouth to Suwannee, Florida. South Florida is not in the warning. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast, Hurricane Simon has 80-knot winds and could reach Category 4 before nearing southwestern Mexico Saturday. Anne Carson’s Nobel Literature win stands from yesterday.

South America. A new Brazilian runoff poll puts Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula in a statistical tie, about 49% to 45%, ahead of the October 25 vote. Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Eduardo Bolsonaro’s prison sentence to begin and issued an arrest warrant, canceling his passports; he is abroad. Brazil recalled its ambassador to Argentina after President Milei’s “Lula ladrón” attack deepened the diplomatic row.

Oceania. A Taxpayers’ Union–Curia poll shows NZ First rising to about 12%, extending the National-led coalition’s lead in New Zealand’s campaign. Australian and New Zealand police hit the Lone Wolf outlaw motorcycle gang with about 20 arrests and 69 charges. Canberra outlined plans to make AI firms prove their safety systems work. Near Queenstown, the Lake Whakatipu scrub fire remains contained.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: MAHA scorecard: 85% broken; White House cites diet wins.
beats.body:
“Make America Healthy Again.” What was done: A scorecard from MAHA activists, including former Kennedy campaign aides, says the administration has broken more than 85% of its food, agriculture, and environmental-health promises—citing new pesticide approvals, a glyphosate supply order, and EPA rollbacks on mercury and some PFAS limits. FDA steps they call only partial include voluntary dye phase-outs and a proposed GRAS-notification rule. The White House points to overhauled dietary guidelines, cutting artificial ingredients, and regenerative-farming investments; HHS says Kennedy is still delivering “lasting reforms.” Impact: the coalition that helped elect the ticket is publicly splitting ahead of the midterms, with some activists saying they may sit out November rather than celebrate unfinished business.

“Lower prescription drug prices.” What was done: The October 22 Customs rule suspending the $800 de minimis exemption for low-value packages still stands, threatening personal Canada and overseas drug orders for about 2.3 million Americans even as most-favored-nation deals and TrumpRx discounts move some list prices. Impact: seniors getting this week’s one-time $90 Part B rebate still see real cash, but MAHA’s own scorekeepers say the bigger chemical-and-food agenda is lagging, and patients who already shop abroad could pay more after the 22nd.

SpaceX. SpaceX agreed Thursday to buy a nationwide portfolio of up to 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management, subject to FCC approval, calling it key for Starlink Mobile to become a U.S. carrier. Musk labeled it a “very big deal.” AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile fell in after-hours trading; SpaceX shares rose about 2.5% after hours. Starlink had about 12 million subscribers as of June and is still the company’s cash engine; Deutsche Bank estimates about 13.5 million by end of September. SpaceX is valued above $2 trillion after its June IPO.

Tesla & honors. Tesla closed near $375 Thursday. At the White House “Science: A New Golden Age” summit, President Trump awarded Musk the National Medal of Science for engineering that pushed space exploration, intelligent systems, and manufacturing; Sergey Brin, Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su also received science medals, with Michael Dell and Satya Nadella getting technology medals. Crew-12’s Dragon return (see NASA) keeps SpaceX’s crew cadence visible to public markets.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City names Sr. Barron; Kramatorsk bus strike; Isaias nears Gulf.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Pope Leo named Sr. Mary Teresa Barron, N.S.A., an Irish missionary sister from Donegal who leads the Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Apostles, as adjunct secretary of the Dicastery for Evangelization’s section for first evangelization and president of the Pontifical Mission Societies, starting January 4, 2027. She led the International Union of Superiors General from 2023 to 2025. This morning he received Sierra Leone’s President Julius Maada Bio, who then met Cardinal Parolin; the talks covered migration-linked environmental and food emergencies, young people, peace, and education. He also received Sydney’s Archbishop Anthony Fisher and Sr. Simona Brambilla, prefect for consecrated life. At 6 p.m. Rome time (noon ET) he celebrates Mass in St. Peter’s to open the pontifical universities’ academic year. A press briefing on the Amoris Laetitia meeting is set for Friday. Archbishop Gallagher is in Pakistan (see Catholic).

Africa. Ethiopian drones hit Eritrean troops around Adigrat in northern Tigray overnight, according to the conflict monitor ACLED and witnesses who spoke to AFP. The two countries cut diplomatic ties last week. Kenya says it still has no Ebola outbreak: one imported case, 57 contacts, 10 in quarantine, and about 17 more traced. Congo’s Bundibugyo outbreak has now killed at least 4,148 people out of 8,300 reported cases. An African Union delegation met M23 rebel leaders and urged them to respect the eastern Congo ceasefire.

Asia. Houthi attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports killed three civilians, a Moroccan, an Algerian, and a Sudanese, and injured 36. Tanker attacks around the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level of the war, at least 12 from September 28 to October 5. Iran and Oman agreed on coordinates for “safe” transit routes, but that is not a full reopening. A Revolutionary Guards commander threatened to block “illegal” southern routes, and Tehran says it will answer U.S. proposals through mediators. In Israel, a Channel 13 poll for the October 27 election puts Netanyahu’s bloc at 55 seats and the opposition at 50, so neither reaches 61. Likud and Eisenkot’s party are tied at 20.

Europe. A Russian glide bomb hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, killing 33 and wounding 18, regional officials say, and the Donetsk region has stopped all public transport. The toll from the Pryluky strike rose to 22, including five children, and three more people were killed in Kyiv today. In France, school blockades resumed despite the prime minister’s promise to act. About 375 schools are closed or disrupted, more than 6,600 people, mostly minors, have been arrested since the protests began, and a large Paris rally is set for today. In Spain, Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction became the symbol of the housing crisis, died in hospital Wednesday. Hundreds marched to parliament, the tenants’ union has called a general strike for November 11, and the snap election is November 29.

North America. Hurricane Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane, has 80 mph winds about 385 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi. It is expected to strengthen and make landfall late Friday or early Saturday between Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and the Florida Panhandle, with storm surge of up to 5 to 7 feet. Florida has declared an emergency in 25 counties and is sending a Miami-based search-and-rescue team, and about a quarter of Gulf oil output is shut in. South Florida is not in the warning area. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast, Tropical Storm Simon could become a major hurricane by the weekend. Minutes from the Fed’s September meeting show the rate hike to 3.75–4% was unanimous and that most officials see another increase as likely by year-end, with several pointing to the AI buildout as a new driver of prices. And Canadian poet Anne Carson, 76, won the Nobel Prize in Literature this morning for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”

South America. In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro says that if elected he will seek sweeping constitutional changes, including judicial reform, a lower age of criminal responsibility, and an end to presidential reelection. Amendments need 308 House votes and 49 in the Senate. Argentina’s President Milei reposted an image of Lula with the words “Lula ladrón” (“Lula thief”), renewing a diplomatic row. In Chile, the Mapocho River burst its banks in Talagante, police airlifted trapped residents, and one person was found dead. Santiago is having its rainiest October in 76 years, blamed on a strong El Niño. Peru’s lower house gave President Keiko Fujimori 90 days of decree powers on security and El Niño, 66–34 with 24 abstaining. The Senate must still ratify.

Oceania. In New Zealand’s election campaign, National’s plan to drug-test unemployed beneficiaries drew fire. Labour and the Greens called it cruel, and Winston Peters warned it “borders on fascist,” while ACT’s David Seymour backed it. In Australia, ministers are sending mixed signals as business groups push back on the tax office’s plan to stop taking credit cards for tax bills from December 1. Near Queenstown, the 1,350-hectare Walter Peak scrub fire is fully contained.

“Lower prescription drug prices.” What was done: The President has signed most-favored-nation pricing deals with drugmakers, and U.S. prescription prices fell 3.1% from a year earlier this summer, though experts credit other factors too. Now a Customs and Border Protection rule takes effect October 22 that indefinitely suspends the $800 “de minimis” exemption for low-value packages. Impact: about 2.3 million Americans buy their drugs abroad, and their orders could be delayed or refused. AP’s example: a three-month supply of the blood thinner Eliquis costs $565 from Canada versus about $1,017 from Amazon. Three Florida Republicans, Reps. Bean, Bilirakis, and Franklin, along with more than 70 Democrats, have asked for protection for personal-use prescriptions. The White House points to its pricing deals. Overall prices are moving the right way, but the Americans already paying the least, many of them Floridians, could end up paying more.

“Bring down health care costs.” What was done: One-time $90 rebates toward Medicare Part B premiums are going out this week, most by direct deposit around Friday, to 20.8 million people in original Medicare. The roughly $2 billion comes from the Medicare Improvement Fund. Impact: it’s real money for millions of seniors, but the roughly 35 million in Medicare Advantage and 12 million low-income beneficiaries are left out, and critics call it a pre-election move. KFF says it “might not go very far.” This is kept as a one-time payment, not a lasting change in costs.

beats.title: Catholic
beats.headline: Bishop Dewane dies; Sr. Barron to lead Mission Societies; Gallagher in Pakistan.
beats.body:
Miami. The Florida Catholic looks back at the Feast of Our Lady of Mercy Mass, held September 24 at Mercy Hospital with students from six archdiocesan schools. The Eucharistic Miracles Exposition opens Monday at St. Mark the Evangelist and runs through Friday. No new clergy assignments posted.

United States. Close to home, Bishop Emeritus Frank J. Dewane of Venice in Florida died Wednesday, the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, at 76. He led the diocese from 2006 until this May. Funeral arrangements are pending. The USCCB also released its November ballot: Bishop Earl Fernandes of Columbus and Bishop Kevin Rhoades of Fort Wayne–South Bend are the nominees for conference secretary.

Latin America. Ahead of Pope Leo’s November trip, Montevideo’s Cardinal Daniel Sturla says the Pope was “impactado,” deeply struck, by youth suicide in Uruguay, which he said needs “an injection of hope.” Uruguay’s visit runs November 6 to 8, and on November 15 in Cusco, Peru, the Pope will celebrate at Sacsayhuamán, give a Golden Rose to the “Mamacha de Belén,” present a pontifical shroud for the “Taytacha de los Temblores,” and meet Quechua-speaking communities.

Europe. French bishops are urging prayer and dialogue as student unrest spreads. “Violence is a failure,” said Bishop Gosselin, and Bishop Olivier de Cagny of Évreux said “violence is unnecessary.”

Africa. Kenya’s Subukia Shrine hosted the bishops’ National Prayer Day for peace ahead of the 2027 election. “Kenya is greater than our differences,” said Archbishop Maurice Muhatia. The day was marked by grief: 17 pilgrims from Mombasa died in a road accident on the way.

Asia. Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s foreign minister, is in Islamabad through Saturday to mark 75 years of Holy See–Pakistan relations. He meets Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, celebrates Mass at Our Lady of Fatima, and visits the Faisal Mosque.

Middle East. In Taybeh, the West Bank’s last entirely Christian village, residents can’t reach their olive trees for the fourth harvest in a row. The village is a closed military zone, which also keeps pilgrims out. Of about 1,200 remaining residents, some 200 are considering leaving, a local activist told Vatican News.

Oceania. Sydney’s Archbishop Anthony Fisher and Auxiliary Bishop Richard Umbers met Pope Leo this morning.

Reassignments.

  • Sr. Mary Teresa Barron, N.S.A., superior general of the Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of the Apostles, becomes adjunct secretary of the Dicastery for Evangelization and president of the Pontifical Mission Societies on January 4, 2027. Born in Donegal in 1968, she led the International Union of Superiors General from 2023 to 2025.
  • Diocese of Venice in Florida (effective October 19): Fr. David M. Vidal leaves Ave Maria Parish to become vicar general, living at Epiphany Cathedral, and Fr. Shawn Roser takes over Ave Maria as administrator. Fr. Daniel Scanlan becomes administrator of Ss. Peter and Paul in Bradenton while pastor Fr. Gordon Zanetti takes medical leave. Fr. Alexander Pince stays vocations director, now living at Resurrection in Fort Myers, and Fr. Jiobani Batista and Fr. Benjamin Casimir become the diocese’s delegates for Hispanic and Haitian ministry (Batista on October 26).
  • Archdiocese of New York: Fr. Christopher Monturo is the new pastor of the Church of the Resurrection in Rye.
  • No other Holy See nominations today, and nothing new in Miami.

beats.title: Signs of the times
beats.headline: Countdown quiet; Rosary message stands; Ghana crusade; Denmark ID breach.
beats.body:
Countdown to the Kingdom. Checked this morning, and nothing new since October 3. The newest posts are still Marija’s Medjugorje message, an Elizabeth Kindelmann Flame of Love passage (“Satan Will be Blinded”), and a Pedro Regis message (“Humanity is Sick”).

Latest message. Our Lady’s September 25 Medjugorje message through Marija is still the newest, and it fits this month of the Rosary: “May this time be a time of prayer for peace. I am calling you to renew in your families the prayer of the Rosary for my intentions, so that I may be able to multiply your prayers and intercede for you before the Most High… I am with you and like never before I pray for you and with you, my little children.” The next monthly message is due October 25.

Eucharistic miracles. No new reports. The Host in Cuilapa, Guatemala, is still under Church investigation, with the bishops urging prudence, and the Eucharistic Miracles Exposition opens in Miami Monday.

Revival and mission. Ghana’s Church of Pentecost reports that its September “Unleashed for Christ” crusade in the Bia area drew a cumulative 23,493 attendees and recorded 1,733 people coming to Christ and 613 water baptisms. In small-town Whitmire, South Carolina, organizers of a late-September crusade describe “a sea of children and youth” crying out to God. In Australia, the Catholic Ignite Conference drew more than 1,300 to Brisbane and will expand to four sites in 2027, including New Zealand for the first time.

Digital ID watch. Denmark is investigating a breach of its Central Person Register. Attackers used a private company’s legitimate access to pull names, addresses, and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million people. It was detected October 2, and a security review has been ordered. It’s a reminder of what’s at stake when a whole nation’s identity sits in one register. No implantable-chip news.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Amoris week underway; Lecornu taps diesel stocks; Ukraine toll 28.
beats.body:
Vatican City. More detail from the first day of the Amoris Laetitia meeting: the 187 participants, including 22 lay people, mostly married couples, sit at 16 round tables in the Paul VI Hall with 26 experts, using the “conversations in the Spirit” method from the synod. Cardinal Farrell’s welcome recalled the Pope’s March message that Familiaris Consortio and Amoris Laetitia “have both strengthened the Church’s doctrinal and pastoral commitment” to young people, couples, and families. In her meditation, Dominican Sr. Helen Alford said Amoris is consistent with the teaching before it, tying both documents to the “law of gradualness,” and said “the beauty of the vocation to marriage is to be found through and with and in its fragility.” Earlier, the Pope told Louisiana’s Patrons of the Arts in the Vatican Museums that “in an age dominated by technology, in which efficiency and profit often take precedence,” we must “allow time and space for beauty.” No new curia appointments since this morning.

Africa. The African Union–backed Africa Credit Rating Agency launched in Port Louis, Mauritius. It is private and self-funded, and governments cannot own shares. Only 32 of Africa’s 55 states are rated by the big three agencies, and the AU says the continent’s external debt service rose from $61 billion in 2010 to $163 billion in 2024.

Asia. Iran’s army spokesman said its forces will carry out pre-emptive operations “should circumstances require it,” and a senior Revolutionary Guard adviser said the Strait of Hormuz “is closed” and will stay that way until Iran’s demands are met. Vice President Vance said it is “not totally clear how their country makes decisions.” In Singapore, smoke from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan pushed air quality into the unhealthy range across all five regions, and fine-particle readings in the west briefly hit the “high” band for the first time this haze season.

Europe. In his address tonight, French Prime Minister Lecornu said France will release 10 million barrels of diesel from its strategic stocks to distributors at cost over three months, which he expects to cut pump prices by 12 to 18 cents a liter. He said electricity prices “must not rise this winter” and asked EDF to maximize production. To students, he said police “have no instruction to confront” them, that their anger “does not come from nowhere,” and that the government’s first decisions will come at the end of October. He held to a 2027 deficit of 5% of GDP and appealed to lawmakers’ “patriotism” to pass a budget. In Ukraine, the toll from Wednesday’s barrage rose to at least 28 dead and 118 injured, including 20 in Pryluky, five of them children. The EU paid out €1.24 billion for Ukrainian-made drones, interceptors, and missiles, and Turkey’s Erdogan told Putin that Turkey is ready to help with direct talks with Ukraine.

North America. Canada’s House of Commons voted down a Conservative motion to end all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day. Only Conservatives voted for it. The Liberal government has already extended its pause on the federal fuel excise tax into 2027.

South America. CBS News reports that federal prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against Venezuela’s former president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing them of torturing more than a dozen Americans held in Venezuelan prisons, possibly as soon as Thursday. Maduro’s lawyer says he has had no notice. Flores has a bond hearing Thursday, and a trial is tentatively set for June 2027.

Oceania. Australia’s High Court, in its first climate case, upheld a ruling that the approval of MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion was invalid, because planners never weighed the local climate effects of emissions from the exported coal. The project must be reassessed, and the ruling affects 17 other New South Wales coal proposals. The mine can keep operating until 2032 under its existing approval, and the NSW Minerals Council called the challenge “activist lawfare.”

beats.headline: Trump Accounts: 70 million kids enrolled; $1,000 seed needs claiming.
beats.body: “A head start for every child” (Trump Accounts, from last year’s tax law). What was done: At the White House today, the President celebrated the automatic enrollment of every eligible child under 18 with a Social Security number, about 70 million accounts. The Treasury’s one-time $1,000 deposit goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028, and parents must claim the account in the Trump Account app to receive it. IRS chief Frank Bisignano said 10 million accounts are funded so far, with $4.5 billion. Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion gift will add $250 for 25 million children, and more than 70 companies, including Uber, Intel, and Nvidia, plan to contribute for employees’ children. Families can add up to $5,000 a year, and the money stays invested until 18. Impact: real money is now landing, but most children already born before 2025 won’t get the federal $1,000, and nothing reaches any child until a parent claims the account. A $1,000 seed growing at the market’s historical average could reach about $5,600 by 18, or roughly $3,600 after taxes and penalties. Kept on paper, and starting to flow.

beats.body: NASA released the full Artemis II lunar science archive: more than 800 gigabytes, including over 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of the crew’s spoken observations, and their annotated notes, along with a preliminary science report. beats.headline: St. Michael School turns 75; Kosovo's first Catholic president; Broome sentencing.
beats.body:
Miami. The Florida Catholic marks 75 years of St. Michael the Archangel School near Little Havana, which now has 325 students from Pre-K3 through eighth grade. Principal Lisette Reina-Naranjo is a 1980 graduate who came back as a parent, volunteer, and teacher. At the anniversary Mass, Archbishop Wenski said, “Whether a family has been a part of the St. Michael family for 60 years or 60 days, the full, transformative measure of Christ’s love, mercy, and education is given equally to all.”

Europe. Kosovo, about 93% Muslim and less than 2% Catholic, elected Justina Shiroka-Pula as its first Catholic president, with 81 votes in parliament. The Kosovo Dispatch notes that her faith “never came up” in a day of hard bargaining.

Oceania. Christopher Saunders, the former bishop of Broome, Australia, was sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men. He will be eligible for parole in 2031, and the Church’s own canonical process is expected to resume. Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian bishops, told the victims, “We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church.”

Other regions. Quiet since noon.

Reassignments. No new Holy See nominations since this morning, and Thursday’s bulletin isn’t out yet. In Little Rock, Bishop Anthony Taylor announced that Fr. Salvador Márquez-Muñoz will retire as pastor of St. Mary in Siloam Springs on October 23. Fr. Emmanuel Torres becomes administrator there, and Fr. Joji Reddy Allam moves to Christ the King in Little Rock and St. Francis of Assisi in Roland. Newark’s October list is mostly pastorate renewals, plus Fr. José Helber Victoria as parochial vicar in Hoboken. Nothing new in Miami.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Pope opens Amoris meeting; India hikes rates; Ukraine toll rises.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Pope Leo opened the Amoris Laetitia meeting this afternoon with a pointed question for the bishops: “What kind of Church, then, do people encounter precisely when they are most fragile?” He named the growing distance between how sex and intimacy are lived and the Christian vision of marriage, and said young people still long for love and fidelity but struggle to believe a lifelong commitment is the way there. He also pointed to economic insecurity, migration, violence, and loneliness, and asked participants to keep “discretion and confidentiality” through the week. Separately, Peoria’s Bishop Louis Tylka presented the Pope with a relic of Blessed Fulton Sheen at a private audience on Monday.

Africa. Kenya’s health minister says the country is not facing an Ebola outbreak, with one imported case, 57 contacts, and 10 in quarantine. Kenya has 241 isolation beds at five hospitals, and officials are meeting Congo, Uganda, and the Africa CDC about how the man crossed three countries undetected. The WHO says the next few days are critical. In Ethiopia, markets reopened in Mekelle after Tigrayan forces pulled out over the weekend, and AP reports government-allied fighters are pushing to retake more ground with drone support.

Asia. The Houthis fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh’s King Khalid airport. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a missile north of the city, and flights were briefly disrupted. India’s central bank raised its key rate a quarter point to 5.5%, its first hike since February 2023, citing the Gulf war and oil prices. Japan asked China to “show proper respect” after a Chinese spokesman referred to Prime Minister Takaichi by name without her title.

Europe. The toll from Russia’s overnight barrage has risen to at least 21 civilians, including four children, with about 60 wounded; 15 died in the Pryluky apartment block. In France, student protests paused today and are expected to resume Thursday, while the 10-year bond yield jumped 16 basis points. Pimco’s CEO told Le Monde “the situation is critical.” Prime Minister Lecornu addresses the nation tonight, with budget talks starting next week.

North America. Mexico’s President Sheinbaum signed a constitutional change requiring candidates for president, governor, or Mexico City mayor to hold only Mexican nationality, starting with the 2028 elections. Dual citizens can keep both passports unless they run for those offices.

South America. In Brazil, Ronaldo Caiado and the Brazil Union–Progressives federation endorsed Flávio Bolsonaro for the October 25 runoff. Flávio said he would use the right’s larger Congress to “change the Constitution,” that his father won’t be in his government and shouldn’t run in 2030, and that he will debate Lula on TV.

Oceania. French Polynesia’s President Moetai Brotherson asked the UN decolonization committee for a visiting mission and a path to a self-determination referendum, with “no predetermined outcome.” France answered that the territory already has broad autonomy.

beats.title: Space
beats.headline: Artemis Accords leaders: Russia, China welcome only if principles align.

Just over 40 countries met behind closed doors and reached agreement on space debris; “the first step… is to stop creating it,” Anderson said. beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City opens Amoris meeting; Israel marks Oct. 7; Russia's huge barrage.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Pope Leo opens the closed-door meeting marking ten years of Amoris Laetitia at 4 p.m. Rome time today in the Paul VI Hall. Cardinals Kevin Farrell and Mario Grech give the welcome, and Dominican Sr. Helen Alford leads a meditation. There are 187 participants, most of them bishops’ conference presidents. There will be no votes, and the synthesis report goes to the Pope rather than replacing the exhortation. It closes with Mass in St. Peter’s Square on October 14. At this morning’s General Audience, on the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, he continued his Gaudium et Spes series. He said the Church’s first mission is to help people face “the profound questions of life,” and that a gap between “professed faith and daily life” is among the gravest errors of our age. He also released a video message ahead of the 100th World Mission Day on October 18, saying evangelization is “always a work of love.” In personnel news, he moved Archbishop Jan Romeo Pawłowski from Greece to be nuncio to Ireland (see Catholic).

Africa. Kenya has identified 57 contacts of its first Ebola patient, who died October 6 after traveling from Congo, and has 10 in quarantine. Doctors Without Borders says spread in Congo’s North Kivu province is “out of control,” with most new cases coming from unknown chains of transmission. In Nigeria, the Air Force named 25 people killed in Monday’s ATR-42 crash in Ondo State and found no survivors. The Senate postponed next week’s security summit in their honor, and the Christian Association of Nigeria is calling for a transparent investigation. Separately, the army says troops repelled an ISWAP assault in Borno State and killed more than 25 fighters.

Asia. Israel is marking three years since the October 7 attack, which killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Ceremonies began at 6:29 a.m. at some 400 sites, and protesters are demanding a state commission of inquiry. It is the first anniversary with all the hostages home. In Gaza, the Hamas-run health ministry counts more than 74,000 dead, and AP reports Israeli strikes continue almost daily despite the ceasefire nearly a year old. In the Gulf, the UK’s maritime agency has logged nine attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz already this month, half of September’s total, even as oil flows near prewar levels and Brent sits just above $101. Vice President Vance told Reuters any deal to reopen the strait would require Iran to cut its ability to enrich uranium. Houthi forces also struck at Aden’s airport. China’s foreign minister told a former Japanese foreign minister that Prime Minister Takaichi herself must resolve her Taiwan remark.

Europe. Russia hit Ukraine overnight with 130 drones and 48 cruise missiles plus ballistic missiles, on Putin’s 74th birthday. At least 15 were killed, with RFE/RL putting the toll at 19, including 13 in a residential building in Pryluky. Ukraine began emergency power cuts in five regions. Kyiv says it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in Russia, and a Liberian-flagged tanker burned off Sochi after a reported naval-drone attack; all 23 Indian crew were rescued. In France, the government suspended stun grenades for school protests after a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off in Lens. More than 250,000 marched Tuesday, more than 500 schools were shut this morning, and Prime Minister Lecornu speaks tonight.

North America. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both closed at record highs Tuesday on AI enthusiasm, with the S&P up 14% this year despite $100 oil and 10-year Treasury yields above 5%. Minutes from the Fed’s September meeting, when it raised rates, come out today. Canada’s Prime Minister Carney announced the first bilateral visit to Türkiye by a Canadian prime minister, October 21 to 23, to push a free-trade deal and energy, mining, and defense ties.

South America. Brazil’s runoff is October 25, with Flávio Bolsonaro at 47.03% to President Lula’s 45.16% in the first round. Lula is overhauling his campaign, shifting to pocketbook attacks over possible cuts to social programs. In Venezuela, a ruptured gas line set off a fire at the Cardón refinery, the country’s second largest. PDVSA shut it down, reported no injuries, and gave no restart date. And Argentina said goodbye to Messi (see Pick-me-up).

Oceania. At the “pre-COP” climate meeting in Nadi, Fiji, Pacific leaders pressed wealthy nations for more help. Papua New Guinea’s Prime Minister Marape said some nations face “being nations no more.” Fiji added $10 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility, which has raised less than half its $500 million goal, and Australia pledged A$3 million for roads and communications in four island nations. Papua New Guinea also committed to help fund Tuvalu’s coastal reclamation. In New Zealand’s election campaign, more than 2,300 voting places were confirmed, Labour promised to take on the big banks, and National unveiled a small-business plan.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Diesel tax relief looks modest; MAHA summit's corporate sponsors rile allies.
beats.body:
“Bring energy prices down.” What was done: Trump signed an order letting a broad range of road vehicles use dyed diesel, which is normally reserved for farm and construction equipment and is exempt from the 24.4-cent federal fuel tax. Federal agencies were also told to defer federal road taxes for the rest of 2026. Impact: small. AAA puts diesel at $6.31 a gallon, up $2.63 (about 70%) from a year ago, mostly because of the Iran war. Analysts told ABC News the tax break takes about $36 off a $948 fill-up of a 150-gallon truck tank, that dyed diesel is sold at few stations, and that the effect on grocery prices will be “negligible.” Some states, including Texas, Nebraska, and North Carolina, added their own waivers. A short-term patch, but the promise of cheaper fuel isn’t being kept right now.

“End the corporate capture of our health agencies.” What was done: At last week’s MAHA Summit, put on by a private group run by Kennedy allies, Kennedy said AI will free Americans from “medical tyranny” by letting them “fact check their own medical advice.” OpenAI and Anthropic were among the sponsors, along with more than a dozen companies with business pending before the government. Sponsors paid up to $300,000, and many got panel slots alongside officials like CMS chief Dr. Oz. Impact: no policy has changed yet, but it’s splitting the movement. Dr. Robert Malone called it “classic pay-to-play,” and medical experts say AI tends to repeat mainstream medical advice, not challenge it. HHS says the goal is helping people understand their own health data alongside their doctors. This one is a credibility test, not a promise kept.

Africa. Ethiopia’s bishops joined Pope Leo’s appeal for dialogue as the new Tigray war spreads. A September 20 drone strike destroyed a food-aid truck from the Eparchy of Adigrat that was headed to a camp for about 56,000 displaced people.

Asia. In India, Bombay’s Auxiliary Bishop Savio Fernandes published “Standing with Gen Z” as young people protest the removal of legitimate voters from electoral rolls. He called for elections that are “impartial, transparent and accountable” and said he wasn’t backing any party.

beats.body:
Vatican City. Pope Leo will go to Assisi on October 27 for the 40th anniversary of St. John Paul II’s 1986 World Day of Prayer for Peace. Sant’Egidio’s gathering there, “Disarmed and Disarming Peace” (a phrase of Pope Leo’s), runs October 25 to 27 with 384 religious and civic representatives from 53 countries. The Pope will pray with Christians in the Lower Basilica, where he and Patriarch Bartholomew will each offer a meditation, then give a message of peace in the piazza. The Vatican also released the full program for tomorrow’s Amoris Laetitia assembly: 187 participants, including 114 bishops’ conference presidents and 22 married couples. Among the Pope’s personal invitees are two bishops from mainland China, whose Party-overseen bishops’ conference the Vatican does not recognize. Pope Leo opens it tomorrow and closes it with Mass in St. Peter’s Square on October 14.

Africa. President Ruto ordered a stepped-up Ebola response in Kenya. Eight family members and 21 health workers are in quarantine, 27 passengers from the flight have been contacted, and 48 people in all are being monitored. Of 267 samples tested, the only positive is still the man who died.

Asia. Israel’s defense minister put the military on high alert ahead of tomorrow’s October 7 anniversary, citing intelligence that Hamas plans attacks on troops in Gaza, and warned Gazans would pay a “heavy price” if soldiers are harmed. In Yemen, Saudi Arabia acknowledged that two of its airports were hit, with three people lightly hurt. Yemeni officials told AP that coalition forces retook the town of Dhubab near the Bab el-Mandeb. The UN migration agency counts more than 184,000 people displaced since August. AP says the U.S. is giving Riyadh intelligence and planning help but isn’t resuming its own strikes.

Europe. Drones hit merchant ships in the Black Sea. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank about 70 miles off Bulgaria, the first reported attack on shipping inside Bulgaria’s economic zone, and its crew is still missing. All 18 crew from the burning Palau-flagged Able were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Zelensky says Ukraine checked with Bulgaria and concluded it was a Russian attack, and Prime Minister Radev called it a “gross violation of international law.” A separate Russian drone strike killed a crew member on a ship carrying rapeseed oil off Odesa.

North America. The big story was Trump launching a new submarine shipyard in Maryland (see Promises). Otherwise quiet since noon.

South America. Argentina is saying goodbye to Messi tonight (see Pick-me-up). In New York, the court hears Cilia Flores’s request for bail and home confinement on Thursday; prosecutors call her an “extreme flight risk.”

Oceania. Fiji’s finance ministry laid out Australia’s 10-year, $1.5 billion package under their Vuvale Union treaty: about $1 billion in grants and $500 million in loans. That includes $284 million to fight transnational crime and drugs and $158 million for health, with the rest going to infrastructure and climate resilience.

Promise in motion, with the payoff in the 2030s.

“Overhaul the childhood vaccine schedule.” What was done: Under Kennedy, the CDC dropped the universal hepatitis B birth dose and moved shots for rotavirus, hepatitis A and B, flu, Covid, RSV, and meningococcal disease to high-risk or “shared decision” status. Kennedy also remade the vaccine advisory panel. In March a federal judge put key changes and the panel’s decisions on hold. On Tuesday, the Justice Department asked the First Circuit to lift that order. Impact: the main changes are frozen in court, and the panel gave no timeline for a ruling. Iran has attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz nearly every day since September 29, and Brent is holding near $100. Separately, Japan said a Chinese survey ship left its economic waters after repeated demands.

Strikes near Moscow killed two men, hurt nine, set a fuel depot on fire, and snarled more than 200 flights. A Russian strike also hit a medical facility in Kramatorsk. European officials tell the Washington Post that Putin is counting on sabotage, cyberattacks, and nuclear threats to break Europe’s support for Kyiv this winter.

South America. Final counts in Brazil show Flávio Bolsonaro with 47.03% to President Lula’s 45.16%, setting up an October 25 runoff. Promise partly kept, with the payoff still ahead.

“The largest deportation operation in history.” What was done: The Marshall Project finds that after the big city operations ended, arrests climbed through a quieter, nationwide approach that relies on about 2,000 local police and sheriff partnerships. DHS reported nearly 51,000 ICE arrests in August, a monthly record. In Florida, July arrests topped 7,000, triple the year before. Impact: arrests are not the same as removals, and in July half of the people arrested had no prior criminal record. That share keeps rising. Enforcement is clearly up, but the deportation total is still not the promised scale.

beats.body:
MAHA: “Find out what’s driving chronic disease, vaccines included.” What was done: Kennedy replaced all 17 voting members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee in June 2025. That panel ended the universal hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation in December. In January the CDC dropped seven vaccines, including flu, RSV, hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, meningococcal, and COVID-19, from the list recommended for every child, moving most of them to “shared clinical decision-making.” Today, at a MAHA Institute event, Kennedy laid out a plan to link Medicare, Medicaid, FDA, and commercial health data for AI-driven studies, with the hepatitis B shot’s timing and aluminum adjuvants high on the list. “We will have answers soon,” he said.

Impact: the policy change is real, but its health effect can’t be measured yet. Today New York joined 15 other states, plus Pennsylvania’s governor, in suing to overturn the schedule and the committee appointments, arguing that the process broke federal law. Some states, New York among them, have already rewritten their school, insurance, and Medicaid rules so they no longer depend on the federal committee. So what a child is offered now depends more on which state they live in. Courts will decide whether the change stands.

United States. On Monday the Pope also met USCCB president Archbishop Paul Coakley and vice president Bishop Daniel Flores, ahead of the Amoris Laetitia meeting October 7 to 14. The Archdiocese of St. Louis sued federal officials and the local sheriff, saying immigrant detainees at the Ste. Genevieve County Jail, most of them Hispanic Catholics, can see priests only by phone through glass. Archbishop Rozanski said that means no confession, Mass, or anointing. The jail’s offer to have a guard pass consecrated hosts in a container was, in his word, “sacrilegious.”

Latin America. Peru is preparing for Pope Leo’s visit November 11 to 16. The Señor de los Milagros image will be at his Lima Mass on November 16.

Africa. The continent’s bishops, through SECAM and Cardinal Ambongo, expressed solidarity with Lusaka’s Archbishop Alick Banda. He was arrested September 28 over a vehicle he says he received as a gift and has since surrendered, and was released on bail. His trial is set for November 3. Zambia’s bishops are also warning about arbitrary arrests since the August election.

Europe, Asia, Middle East, Oceania. Nothing bigger than what noon covered. The Korea and Gaza items are under World and noon’s Catholic beat.

Reassignments. Cardinal Mauro Gambetti, 60, a Conventual Franciscan, moves from St. Peter’s Basilica to Archbishop of Chieti-Vasto. He succeeds Archbishop Bruno Forte, 77, who retired at the age limit. Bishop Peter J. Byrne’s resignation as auxiliary bishop of New York was accepted. Msgr. Grzegorz Bielaszka, 52, a Polish Vatican diplomat who has served in Panama, Iraq, Hungary, Peru, and Gabon, was named nuncio to the United Arab Emirates and made an archbishop. Nothing new for Miami or Florida.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Ethiopia retakes Mekelle; Iran oil minister resigns; Brazil runoff set.
beats.body:
Africa. Ethiopian federal forces and an allied militia retook Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, after the TPLF pulled out; it’s the worst fighting since the 2020–22 war and has spread into Afar. Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan put out a joint call for peaceful solutions, while all deny Ethiopia’s charge that they’re backing the rebels.

Antarctica. New research says the continent will keep losing ice this century even if emissions are cut, though lower emissions shrink the loss. No acute event.

Asia. Iran’s oil minister resigned as the economy buckles under the blockade, with inflation around 85% and a 10% contraction early this year. Separately, the ICC unveiled arrest warrants for Taliban supreme leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani.

Europe. Russia’s jet-powered drones are now going after bridges in Kyiv, an escalation after more than a month of round-the-clock strikes on the capital.

North America. The Supreme Court opened its new term today. The first case argued asks whether federal law blocks state climate-damage suits against energy companies (Suncor v. Boulder County).

South America. Brazil heads to an October 25 runoff. Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round with 47.0% to Lula’s 45.2%, which was better than polls expected for the right.

Oceania. Fiji is hosting the Pacific pre-COP climate meeting with Australia and Tuvalu ahead of COP31. Fiji also set a possible December 9 referendum on a new constitution.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Food-dye phase-out stays voluntary; deportation drive still short of target.
beats.body:
MAHA: “Get synthetic dyes out of our food.” The promise: phase out petroleum-based dyes. What was done: voluntary industry pledges and an FDA list of companies that signed on, but no new rule more than a year later; only the already-scheduled Red No. 3 ban (effective January 2027) carries legal force. Impact: some reformulation by brands that pledged, but nothing binding, and AP reports a future administration could easily undo it.

MAHA: “Define and rein in ultra-processed food; fix school meals.” What was done: per the Wall Street Journal, as summarized today by the Food Institute, the White House has repeatedly held back Kennedy’s ultra-processed food definition and the USDA school-meal overhaul over lawsuit and trade worries. Impact: none yet. This one is stalled inside the administration, not kept.

MAGA: “Largest deportation operation in history.” What was done: about $70 billion for ICE and CBP, a much bigger ICE workforce, local-police arrest authority, and the end of several TPS designations. Impact: record ICE arrests, but ICE’s own count was about 356,000 removals through July, well short of a million a year. At least 51% of July arrestees had no criminal conviction or charge. PolitiFact rates it “In the Works.”

beats.title: Musk world
beats.headline: Tesla Q3 deliveries beat consensus; Starship Flight 15 eyed mid-October.
beats.body:
Tesla. Shares rose for a second day, to about $377–378 this morning, after Q3 deliveries of 486,532 beat the roughly 462,000 consensus. That’s still down 2.1% from last year, and Tesla sold about 22,000 more cars than it built, so some of the beat came from clearing inventory. Energy storage deployments were 13.7 GWh. The real test is Q3 earnings after the close on October 21. Watch margins excluding regulatory credits and how much was discounted.

SpaceX. Following Starship’s first orbital flight on September 28 (26 Starlink V3 satellites deployed), Flight 15 is penciled in for no earlier than October 19 and may try the first tower catch of a Ship. Flight 16, a possible first Starship launch from Kennedy’s pad 39A, is provisionally no earlier than October 30. Neither date is official yet.

beats.title: Space
beats.headline: NASA pauses Blue Origin Mars orbiter after Rocket Lab protest.
beats.body: NASA has reportedly paused Blue Origin’s Mars Telecommunications Orbiter contract after Rocket Lab filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office over the award. Meanwhile, Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket looks increasingly likely to slip its first flight to 2027. The International Astronautical Congress opened today in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs through Friday, with ESA’s chief and China’s space agency at the leaders’ sessions.

beats.title: NASA
beats.headline: Artemis III Earth-orbit test waits on both landers; KSC layoffs set.
beats.body: Administrator Jared Isaacman says next year’s Artemis III Earth-orbit test won’t fly unless both landers, SpaceX’s Starship and Blue Origin’s, are ready. A crewed landing is still targeted for 2028, with China aiming for 2029–30. His deputy, Matt Anderson, told reporters at the congress that NASA has “exciting news to announce very soon.” Closer to home, contractor Amentum will lay off 70 Kennedy Space Center workers on November 30 as NASA brings core technical jobs in-house.

beats.title: Catholic
beats.headline: Pope Leo prays for Gaza victims and urges valuing women's work.
beats.body: Pope Leo sent a personal message to Gaza’s Catholic parish priest after an Israeli strike killed five civilians, praying, “How long, O Lord?” Meeting Vatican lay employees today, he said women’s contributions must be increasingly recognized and that AI cannot replace human work. No new Miami or Florida clergy assignments have been posted since the summer appointments.

beats.title: Signs of the times
beats.headline: Medjugorje September 25 message urges daily Rosary for peace.
beats.body:
Countdown to the Kingdom posted three new items over the weekend that this morning missed. The headline post is Our Lady’s September 25 Medjugorje message through Marija, still the latest monthly message and now distributed with ecclesiastical approval. In it she asks families to renew the daily Rosary for her intentions, so that she can intercede for peace, adding, “like never before I pray for you and with you.”

That lines up closely with Pope Leo’s October Rosary call. The other two posts are a Flame of Love passage from Elizabeth Kindelmann (“the Spirit of Pentecost will flood the earth”) and an October 2 message to Pedro Regis (“healing will come, only by the mercy of Jesus”). No new verified Eucharistic miracle reports turned up.

beats.body: Star Wars: Galactic Racer launches tomorrow, October 6, on PS5, Xbox, and PC. It’s a run-based racer with speeders and swoop bikes through Jakku’s Star Destroyer graveyard, and yes, Sebulba shows up. On the Heat side, Spoelstra compared Giannis’s passing to Magic Johnson after Saturday’s preseason win. There’s an intrasquad scrimmage Tuesday, and the season opens October 21 against Minnesota.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Iran war in eighth month; Hormuz closed; G7 releases oil stocks.
beats.body:
The Iran war is in its eighth month. The Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous: another tanker was hit over the weekend, and Tehran says the strait stays closed until U.S. conditions are met. Oil eased after the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months—Brent around $101–102, U.S. crude near $90—though diesel and shipping costs stay high.

An Iranian security official admitted the economy is in one of its worst stretches under the U.S. blockade. In Ukraine, Russia launched more than 1,900 drones last week; Kyiv says it is open to U.S.-backed talks late this month but remains short on funding. U.S. futures opened slightly lower ahead of Fed minutes on Wednesday.

beats.title: Catholic
beats.headline: Pope Leo asks daily October Rosary for peace, especially Holy Land.
beats.body: Pope Leo has asked the faithful to pray the Rosary every day in October for an end to wars, especially in the Holy Land. At the Vatican, a gathering of families and young people runs October 7–14 marking ten years of Amoris Laetitia. Closer to home, Archbishop Wenski marked Little Flower’s 100th anniversary and Amor en Acción’s 50th.

beats.body: Giannis made his first Heat appearance Saturday: Miami beat Toronto 129–105. He had 9 points and 7 assists in about 14 minutes, then rested the second half. Next up: New Orleans on Thursday.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Russia to intensify Ukraine strikes; Houthis claim Aramco hit near Riyadh.
beats.body:
Russia said it would intensify strikes on Ukraine after a Zelenskiy interview outlining further attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. Separately, the U.S. told France and Germany to release diesel stocks or face a U.S. export ban—pressure that Zero Hedge also covered as Europe’s emergency supplies came into focus.

In the Gulf, Houthis claimed a strike on an Aramco facility near Riyadh; Saudi forces hit Sanaa in response. Hormuz and Red Sea routes remain the quiet pressure behind every oil headline.

beats.title: Catholic
beats.headline: Wenski marks Little Flower centennial; Pope Leo points to Saint Francis.
beats.body: Archbishop Wenski marked Little Flower’s centennial and Amor en Acción’s fiftieth—local roots and missionary discipleship side by side. From Rome, Pope Leo’s Angelus pointed to Saint Francis as a path to build peace, and the Vatican previewed a gathering for a new proclamation of the Gospel with families on the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia.
